title: Harun al-Rashid
hook: the caliph of the Thousand and One Nights legends, and of real scholars and envoys

segments.voice: Yesterday, Madinat al-Salam, al-Mansur's Baghdad, drawn in lines of fire on the bank of the Tigris. Your line was: a circle, drawn in fire. What did you find at the center of your circle? Day nine hundred fourteen.

A caliph slips out of his palace at night, dressed as a merchant. With him are his vizier, Ja'far, and his swordbearer, Masrur. They wander the lanes of Baghdad, overhear a fisherman's troubles, knock on a strange door, and stumble into an adventure that ends with the caliph revealing who he is and setting everything right. That's Harun al-Rashid as readers have long met him, in the stories of the Thousand and One Nights. But there was a real Harun, who ruled from Baghdad, and the real one left traces in histories, law books, and even the records of a king in Europe. Today: telling the two apart.
screen: `A CALIPH IN DISGUISE.` → `JA'FAR AND MASRUR.` → `THE STORIES, AND THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Start with what the histories say. Al-Tabari records that Harun led pilgrimages to Mecca and also led campaigns against the Byzantine empire on his frontier. His wife Zubayda is remembered for paying for wells and water stations along the pilgrim road from Iraq. Then the scholars. The jurist Abu Yusuf, a student of Abu Hanifa, wrote a book on taxation and public finance addressed to Harun, advising him how to collect revenue fairly. Then the envoys. Annals kept at the court of Charlemagne, the Frankish ruler, record that Harun's embassy brought Charlemagne gifts, among them an elephant, named Abul Abaz. Now the hardest real story. Ja'far, the friendly vizier of the tales, was a real man, from the powerful Barmakid family who helped run the empire. The histories report that Harun suddenly had Ja'far executed and brought the whole family down. They give different reasons, and the cause is still uncertain. So the real Harun was pious and warlike, generous and frightening, a patron of scholars and a ruler who could destroy his closest friend overnight. The tales soften him into the wise night-walker who fixes everything. Both versions have their uses. The stories are wonderful stories. But they are not evidence. Holding them apart is a skill: enjoy the legend as legend, and read history as history, with its gaps and its blood left in. Legend and history.
screen: `PILGRIM AND SOLDIER.` · `A LAW BOOK ADDRESSED TO HIM.` · `AN ELEPHANT FOR CHARLEMAGNE.` · then, large: `THE FALL OF THE BARMAKIDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: separate legend from history. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind a story you've heard told about someone famous, or about your own family: the grandparent who did something remarkable, the founder who started with nothing. Breathe in. Ask: what do I actually know happened? Breathe out. Ask: what has been polished in the telling? You don't need to throw the story away. Just hold the two piles side by side, the known and the told. If you pray, you can ask for honesty in how you tell your own stories. The bell holds the time.
Harun al-Rashid. The Abbasid caliph of the Thousand and One Nights tales, and the real ruler of pilgrimages, campaigns, scholars, envoys and the sudden fall of the Barmakids. Today's word.
Your line: legend and history. Today, when you hear a story about someone, ask yourself once: is this the legend or the history? Day nine hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Readers around the world still enjoy the Thousand and One Nights as story, while historians read al-Tabari, Abu Yusuf's book on taxation and the Frankish annals to reconstruct the real Harun.

fork.setup: you're a historian. a tale says Harun walked Baghdad in disguise and set every wrong right. what do you do with it?
options: enjoy it as a tale, and look for the history elsewhere.
fork.reveal: the tales are stories; the real Harun is found in al-Tabari, Abu Yusuf's book and the Frankish annals, gaps and all.

original.note: Arabic: the rightly guided one, the title Harun ruled under.

trapdoor: what you thought: the fairy-tale caliph who walked Baghdad in disguise.
what it means: a real ruler, pious, warlike and feared, whom the tales later softened.
what a scholar hears: al-Tabari's report of the fall of the Barmakids, Abu Yusuf's book on taxation, and the elephant in the Frankish annals.

sources.ref: al-Tabari, Tarikh (Harun's pilgrimages and campaigns; the execution of Ja'far and the fall of the Barmakids)
